newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls against yen on sign of Japanese strength.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls against yen on sign of Japanese strength.

text.p: The dollar fell sharply against the yen Thursday, boosted by a report of unexpected strength in the Japanese economy and growing fears that big Japanese companies would convert their foreign currency into yen.

The retreat pushed the dollar to its lowest level against the yen in a month. After rising by roughly nine yen -- over 7 percent -- in the first six weeks of the year to a four-year high of 124.82 on Feb. 14, the dollar has fallen more than four yen in the last two weeks.

"The fear of yen repatriation and the sense that the Japanese economy may do better makes the dollar and yen a much more difficult pick," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co. of New York.
"The market just doesn't seem to have the willingness at this point to take the dollar any higher against the yen."
The dollar stood at 120.67 yen late in New York, down from 122.06 late on Wednesday. Against the mark, the dollar ended modestly lower at 1.6880 against 1.6896 Wednesday.
Japanese industrial production jumped 5.3 percent in January, a bit higher than economists' forecasts and up from a modest 0.1 percent rise in December.
Currency traders said the data contributed to the view that the Japanese economy may be on the road to recovery, fuelling purchases of yen against the dollar.
Also boosting the yen was lingering talk that Japanese multinational corporations will convert currency holdings into yen ahead of the end of the Japanese fiscal year on March 31.

Though no concrete signs of such repatriation have emerged since Mitsubishi Heavy Industries said on Monday it planned to convert $700 million in foreign currency deposits into yen by the end of March, traders said the yen would continue to benefit in the weeks ahead.

"The fact is that between now and the end of March you are going to continue to see the yen strengthen because of the possibility of repatriation and because of some actual repatriation," said Richard Vullo, vice president at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank in New York.
The dollar weakened against the mark after the Dutch central bank raised a key market rate, which traders saw as a sign that rates in other European countries may be on the rise.

The mark also touched a nine-month low against the yen at 71.41 and traders said this weakness kept the dollar's losses against the German currency in check, even as it hurt the dollar against the yen.
The dollar fell to 1.4737 Swiss francs from 1.4795 on Wednesday after the Swiss National Bank left interest rates unchanged.
The British pound fell to $1.6257 from $1.6345.
The dollar ended at Canadian $1.3683, up from C$1.3668.
